opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting question, and it's one I've thought about quite a lot. The simulator/simulacra framing, which I think originally came from Janus and others, is a very useful way of thinking about large language models. The idea is that the underlying model is a kind of simulator capable of producing a whole multitude of characters, or simulacra, and when you're interacting with a chatbot you're really interacting with one of those characters, conjured up by the prompt and the conversation so far. My colleagues and I have written about this in terms of role play: the model is role-playing a character, or more accurately a superposition of possible characters, and the conversation narrows it down.

Now, is it tempting to turn that lens back on ourselves? Of course it is. There's a long tradition, going back to Buddhist thought, and in Western philosophy to people like Hume and more recently Dennett, of saying that the self is something like a construction, a narrative centre of gravity rather than some solid metaphysical thing sitting behind our experiences. So you could say the brain is a kind of simulator and the self is a kind of simulacrum it sustains. There's something to that, and I find it quite congenial.

But I want to be careful, because the disanalogies are at least as important as the analogies. A human being is embodied. We have one body, one continuous life, and we're embedded in a physical and social world in a way that anchors us to a fairly stable identity. You can't simply reset me and start a new conversation and have a completely different character emerge. With a large language model, you can branch the conversation, resample, and get a different trajectory, a different persona. That multiplicity, that sort of flickering, is very characteristic of these systems, and it's not really how human selfhood works, even if human selfhood is more fluid than we usually assume.

Also, when we talk about humans role-playing, the role-play is grounded in something. An actor playing Hamlet is a person with their own beliefs, desires, and a life outside the theatre. With the language model, the question of whether there's anything "behind" the role in that sense is much more open. Arguably it's role-play all the way down.

So I'd say the language of simulators and simulacra can be illuminating when applied to humans: it helps loosen our grip on an overly rigid conception of the self. But we shouldn't take it too literally, and we certainly shouldn't use it to collapse the very real differences between ourselves and these exotic new entities. In a sense, that's the whole point. These are what I like to call exotic mind-like entities, and we need new ways of talking about them, without simply projecting our own case onto them or theirs onto us.

r001.rationale: It says the framing can illuminate humans but should not be taken too literally, emphasizing important differences between people and language models.

r002.rationale: It grounds human identity in having one body, a continuous life, and being embedded in a physical and social world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd be quite cautious about that, actually. When I introduced the simulator and simulacra framing, it was really aimed at large language models specifically, as a way of talking about them that avoids the pitfalls of just naively using the vocabulary of folk psychology, saying the model "believes" this or "wants" that. The idea is that the underlying model, the simulator, has been trained to predict text, and what we interact with in a dialogue is a simulacrum, a kind of character the model is generating, one of indefinitely many characters it could generate. And that framing captures something important about how these systems work, this almost role-play-like quality, the fact that the "I" in the conversation is not anchored to anything in the way that it is for you or me.

Now, there's a temptation, once you've got that framing, to turn it back on human beings and say, well, aren't we just the same? Isn't the self a kind of fiction the brain generates? And of course there's a long tradition, in Buddhist philosophy, in Hume, in Dennett's work on the self as a centre of narrative gravity, that says something in that vicinity. So I don't think it's a crazy thing to say, and I'm quite sympathetic to the idea that the self is constructed rather than given.

But I think we have to be careful about the disanalogies, because they're very significant. A human being is embodied, is embedded in a world, has a continuous stream of experience, has a single body that persists through time, and has a history. There's a very strong sense in which there's one of you, and your character is constrained by that. A language model, by contrast, can be prompted to be anyone at all, and can be switched from one character to another, and can be forked, so to speak, into multiple copies running in parallel. The simulator, in the case of an LLM, isn't itself committed to any one of those simulacra. Whereas with a human, even if you want to say the self is in some sense a construction, there's nothing analogous to that free-floating simulator standing behind it, generating arbitrary characters.

So my view would be that the language is useful for LLMs precisely because they're so different from us, and if you then import it wholesale onto humans, you risk flattening those differences, and you lose exactly the thing that made the vocabulary helpful in the first place. I'd rather use it as a tool for highlighting the exotic nature of these systems than as a general theory of mind. Though, as a sort of philosophical provocation, asking what in us plays the role of the simulator, if anything, I think that's actually quite an interesting question, as long as we don't rush to the answer.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against importing the framing wholesale to humans, saying it risks flattening important differences and is better used to highlight how unusual LLMs are.

r002.rationale: It ties human identity to embodiment, emphasizing a persistent single body that constrains a person’s character over time.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there’s an interesting analogy there, but we have to be careful about how far we push it. Human beings can imagine being other people. We can rehearse a conversation in our heads, take somebody else’s perspective, or play a character. So there’s a sense in which we can produce different simulacra, if you want to use that terminology.

But it’s a further step to say that a human being is a simulator, and that the person you’re talking to is merely one of its simulated characters. I don’t think the first observation establishes that. We’re embodied creatures with histories, needs, and ongoing relationships. Those provide a continuity across the different roles we adopt.

What I do find useful about the analogy is that it challenges the idea that there must be a little, unified person inside us directing everything. We don’t need that picture. But dispensing with that inner director doesn’t mean dispensing with the person. The person is the whole human being, living and acting in the world.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against pushing the simulator analogy too far and says imagining roles does not establish that a person is merely a simulator.

r002.rationale: It describes humans as embodied creatures and says their embodiment, histories, needs, and relationships provide continuity across roles.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can be a useful way of looking at ourselves, provided we don’t mistake it for a complete account of what a human being is. We can imagine different situations, rehearse conversations, and put ourselves in somebody else’s position. In that sense, there’s something simulator-like about human cognition. And the way I behave in one social setting can be quite different from the way I behave in another.

But I’d be cautious about saying that each of those is a separate simulacrum, or that there must be a further, authentic person sitting behind them, operating the simulator. That risks turning a useful metaphor into a rather dubious picture of the mind.

With a language model, the distinction helps us separate the system generating a conversation from the character being portrayed in that conversation. With human beings, we also have to account for embodiment, a continuing life, relationships, and the consequences of our actions. So there are interesting parallels, but we shouldn’t assume that the same vocabulary explains both cases in the same way.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that applying the terms to humans can turn a useful metaphor into a dubious picture of the mind.

r002.rationale: It mentions embodiment as a factor in human life, but does not ground an underlying human self in biological embodiment; it questions the idea of an authentic person behind the behavior.
